claim: The ability to speak coherently is essential for effective communication but declines with age.
source: The ability to speak coherently is essential for effective communication but declines with age: older people more frequently produce tangential, off-topic speech.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Older people more frequently produce tangential, off-topic speech.
source: The ability to speak coherently is essential for effective communication but declines with age: older people more frequently produce tangential, off-topic speech.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Semantic selection ability predicted coherence in speech.
source: Semantic selection ability predicted coherence, as did level of semantic knowledge and a measure of domain-general executive ability.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the study's data analysis.

claim: Level of semantic knowledge predicted coherence in speech.
source: Semantic selection ability predicted coherence, as did level of semantic knowledge and a measure of domain-general executive ability.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the study's data analysis.

claim: Domain-general executive ability predicted coherence in speech.
source: Semantic selection ability predicted coherence, as did level of semantic knowledge and a measure of domain-general executive ability.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the study's data analysis.

claim: Semantic and executive factors fully accounted for the age-related coherence deficit.
source: These factors fully accounted for the age-related coherence deficit.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on statistical modeling.

claim: Maintaining coherence in speech becomes more challenging as people age because they accumulate more knowledge but are less able to effectively regulate how it is activated and used.
source: Our results indicate that maintaining coherence in speech becomes more challenging as people age because they accumulate more knowledge but are less able to effectively regulate how it is activated and used.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: Discourse that successfully navigates conversational challenges is said to be coherent.
source: Discourse that successfully navigates these challenges is said to be coherent: it consists of a series of well-connected statements all related to a shared topic, making it easy to comprehend (Foltz, 2007; Glosser and Deser, 1992).
evidence: This is a definition provided with supporting citations.

claim: Coherent discourse consists of a series of well-connected statements all related to a shared topic, making it easy to comprehend.
source: Discourse that successfully navigates these challenges is said to be coherent: it consists of a series of well-connected statements all related to a shared topic, making it easy to comprehend (Foltz, 2007; Glosser and Deser, 1992).
evidence: This is a definition provided with supporting citations.

claim: Older adults are more likely to produce tangential, off-topic utterances in conversation.
source: Older adults are more likely to produce tangential, off-topic utterances in conversation (Arbuckle and Gold, 1993; Glosser and Deser, 1992)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Older adults provide irrelevant information when telling a story.
source: and to provide irrelevant information when telling a story (Juncos-Rabadán et al., 2005; Marini et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Older adults provide irrelevant information when describing an object.
source: or describing an object (Long et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Changes in coherence reduce the effectiveness of communication and the quality of older people's verbal interactions.
source: Such changes reduce the effectiveness of communication and the quality of older people's verbal interactions (Arbuckle et al., 2000; Pushkar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Less coherent speech is associated with higher levels of stress in social interactions.
source: Indeed, less coherent speech is associated with higher levels of stress and less satisfaction in social interactions (Arbuckle and Gold, 1993; Gold et al., 1988; Pushkar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Less coherent speech is associated with less satisfaction in social interactions.
source: Indeed, less coherent speech is associated with higher levels of stress and less satisfaction in social interactions (Arbuckle and Gold, 1993; Gold et al., 1988; Pushkar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Local coherence is the degree to which adjoining utterances relate meaningfully to one another.
source: Researchers have often made a distinction between local coherence (LC), the degree to which adjoining utterances relate meaningfully to one another, and global coherence (GC), the degree to which each utterance relates to the topic under discussion (Glosser and Deser, 1992; Kintsch and van Dijk, 1978).
evidence: This is a definition provided with supporting citations.

claim: Global coherence is the degree to which each utterance relates to the topic under discussion.
source: Researchers have often made a distinction between local coherence (LC), the degree to which adjoining utterances relate meaningfully to one another, and global coherence (GC), the degree to which each utterance relates to the topic under discussion (Glosser and Deser, 1992; Kintsch and van Dijk, 1978).
evidence: This is a definition provided with supporting citations.

claim: Most studies have reported larger declines in global coherence in later life.
source: Most studies have reported larger declines in GC in later life, though reductions in LC have also been observed (Glosser and Deser, 1992; Kemper et al., 2010; Marini et al., 2005; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous research with supporting citations.

claim: Reductions in local coherence have been observed in later life.
source: Most studies have reported larger declines in GC in later life, though reductions in LC have also been observed (Glosser and Deser, 1992; Kemper et al., 2010; Marini et al., 2005; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous research with supporting citations.

claim: Explanations for age-related decline in coherence have typically focused on deterioration in domain-general cognitive control processes.
source: Explanations for age-related decline in coherence have typically focused on deterioration in domain-general cognitive control processes, which are assumed to be involved in the monitoring and selection of topics during speech (Kintz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous theoretical approaches with a supporting citation.

claim: Domain-general cognitive control processes are assumed to be involved in the monitoring and selection of topics during speech.
source: Explanations for age-related decline in coherence have typically focused on deterioration in domain-general cognitive control processes, which are assumed to be involved in the monitoring and selection of topics during speech (Kintz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption in the literature with a supporting citation.

claim: Coherence in speech is predicted by performance on non-verbal tasks requiring cognitive control.
source: This view is supported by a handful of studies reporting that coherence in speech is predicted by performance on non-verbal tasks requiring cognitive control (Gold et al., 1988; Kintz et al., 2016; North et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Declines in coherence result from a reduced ability to inhibit irrelevant information.
source: One particular theory holds declines in coherence result from a reduced ability to inhibit irrelevant information, which means that older people are less able to prevent irrelevant or off-topic ideas from intruding into their discourse (Arbuckle and Gold, 1993; Marini and Andreetta, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a theory from the literature with supporting citations.

claim: Performance on cognitive tests requiring inhibition predicts the level of coherence in older adults' speech.
source: This view is supported by evidence that performance on cognitive tests requiring inhibition, such as the Stroop test and Trails test, predicts the level of coherence in older adults' speech (Arbuckle and Gold, 1993; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Inhibition does not provide a complete explanation for age-related coherence declines.
source: However, this factor does not appear to provide a complete explanation for age-related coherence declines.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the literature review.

claim: Previous studies have overlooked the critical role that conceptual knowledge about the world plays in the generation of meaningful, coherent speech.
source: This is likely because previous studies have overlooked the critical role that conceptual knowledge about the world (i.e., semantic knowledge) plays in the generation of meaningful, coherent speech.
evidence: This is stated as a critique of previous research and a motivation for the current study.

claim: Coherence depends on the ability to regulate the activation of semantic knowledge.
source: Here, we propose and test the hypothesis that coherence depends not only on domain-general executive resources, but specifically on the ability to regulate the activation of semantic knowledge, ensuring that only the most relevant concepts are selected for inclusion in speech.
evidence: This is stated as the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: All propositional speech relies on the retrieval and use of semantic knowledge.
source: All propositional speech relies on the retrieval and use of semantic knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as a foundational principle.

claim: The selection of words for production is guided by their meaning.
source: This is true at the lexical level, since the selection of words for production is guided by their meaning.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about language production.

claim: The content of speech is informed by general semantic knowledge about the topic under discussion.
source: But it is also true at the broader conceptual level, as the content of our speech is informed by our general semantic knowledge about the topic under discussion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about language production.

claim: The coherence of an individual's discourse is critically determined by the quality of the semantic knowledge they have on the topic under discussion.
source: Thus, the coherence of an individual's discourse is likely to be critically determined by (a) the quality of the semantic knowledge they have on the topic under discussion and (b) by their ability to retrieve and select the most appropriate information to talk about.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical prediction based on reasoning about semantic processing.

claim: The coherence of an individual's discourse is critically determined by their ability to retrieve and select the most appropriate information to talk about.
source: Thus, the coherence of an individual's discourse is likely to be critically determined by (a) the quality of the semantic knowledge they have on the topic under discussion and (b) by their ability to retrieve and select the most appropriate information to talk about.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical prediction based on reasoning about semantic processing.

claim: Representations of semantic knowledge are centred on the anterior temporal cortices.
source: Current theories hold that representations of semantic knowledge are centred on the anterior temporal cortices and that a separate 'semantic control' system provides top-down regulation of the activation and selection of concepts from this store, based on current situational demands (Badre and Wagner, 2002; Hoffman et al., 2018; Jefferies, 2013; Jefferies and Lambon Ralph, 2006; Ralph et al., 2017; Yee and Thompson-Schill, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as current theoretical knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: A separate 'semantic control' system provides top-down regulation of the activation and selection of concepts from the semantic store.
source: Current theories hold that representations of semantic knowledge are centred on the anterior temporal cortices and that a separate 'semantic control' system provides top-down regulation of the activation and selection of concepts from this store, based on current situational demands (Badre and Wagner, 2002; Hoffman et al., 2018; Jefferies, 2013; Jefferies and Lambon Ralph, 2006; Ralph et al., 2017; Yee and Thompson-Schill, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as current theoretical knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The semantic store and semantic control system can be independently impaired following brain damage.
source: These principal components of semantic cognition – the store of representations and the control system – can be independently impaired following brain damage (Jefferies, 2013; Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Some aspects of semantic control are impaired in later life.
source: Importantly for the present study, recent evidence suggests some aspects of semantic control are impaired in later life.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from recent research.

claim: Older people have a broader vocabulary than young people.
source: In common with many previous studies, older people were found to have a broader vocabulary, indicating a richer repository of semantic knowledge (Grady, 2012; Nilsson, 2003; Nyberg et al., 1996; Park et al., 2002; Rönnlund et al., 2005; Salthouse, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Hoffman (2018) consistent with previous research, with supporting citations.

claim: Older people have a richer repository of semantic knowledge than young people.
source: In common with many previous studies, older people were found to have a broader vocabulary, indicating a richer repository of semantic knowledge (Grady, 2012; Nilsson, 2003; Nyberg et al., 1996; Park et al., 2002; Rönnlund et al., 2005; Salthouse, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from vocabulary findings with supporting citations.

claim: No age differences were found for the ability to engage in controlled search of the semantic knowledge store to detect weak associations between concepts.
source: The first task probed the ability to engage in controlled search of the semantic knowledge store to detect weak associations between concepts. No age differences were found for this ability.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Hoffman (2018).

claim: Older adults were less successful than young people at selecting among competing semantic associations.
source: The second tested the ability to select among competing semantic associations (hereafter termed semantic selection). The semantic selection task required participants to inhibit prepotent but irrelevant semantic information in favour of task-relevant aspects of knowledge. Older adults were less successful than young people, indicating age-related decline in this aspect of semantic control.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Hoffman (2018).

claim: Age-related decline in controlled selection of semantic information is consistent with reduced activity in the left prefrontal region in older adults.
source: Evidence for age-related decline in controlled selection of semantic information is consistent with a meta-analysis of 47 functional neuroimaging studies indicating that older adults show reduced activity in the left prefrontal region most strongly linked with this ability (Hoffman and Morcom, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence from a meta-analysis with a citation.

claim: Older adults show reduced activity in the left prefrontal region most strongly linked with semantic selection ability.
source: Evidence for age-related decline in controlled selection of semantic information is consistent with a meta-analysis of 47 functional neuroimaging studies indicating that older adults show reduced activity in the left prefrontal region most strongly linked with this ability (Hoffman and Morcom, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a meta-analysis with a citation.

claim: The ability to select task-relevant semantic representations may be crucial in speech production because it may allow people to select the most relevant aspects of knowledge for use in speech.
source: The ability to select task-relevant semantic representations may be crucial in speech production because it may allow people to select the most relevant aspects of knowledge for use in speech and thus to avoid irrelevant shifts in topic.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical prediction.

claim: Young people were faster to respond in the Trails test than older people.
source: Young people were faster to respond in the Trails test and produced more items in category fluency.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's cognitive assessments.

claim: Young people produced more items in category fluency than older people.
source: Young people were faster to respond in the Trails test and produced more items in category fluency.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's cognitive assessments.

claim: Older people produced slightly more words in letter fluency than young people.
source: Older people produced slightly more words in letter fluency, however.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's cognitive assessments.

claim: There were no group differences in MMSE scores.
source: There were no group differences in MMSE scores, with all participants scoring at least 26/30.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's cognitive assessments.

claim: All participants scored at least 26/30 on the MMSE.
source: There were no group differences in MMSE scores, with all participants scoring at least 26/30.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's cognitive assessments.

claim: The older group scored significantly higher on the vocabulary tests of semantic knowledge.
source: The older group scored significantly higher on the vocabulary tests of semantic knowledge, indicating that they had a broader set of verbal semantic information available to them.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's semantic assessments.

claim: Older people had a broader set of verbal semantic information available to them than young people.
source: The older group scored significantly higher on the vocabulary tests of semantic knowledge, indicating that they had a broader set of verbal semantic information available to them.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the vocabulary test findings.

claim: The manipulation of association strength had similar effects in young and older people.
source: Controlled retrieval was assessed by manipulating association strength during semantic judgements, since the detection of weak associations requires greater control over the retrieval of information from semantic memory (Badre and Wagner, 2007). This manipulation had similar effects in young and older people, suggesting that the ability to retrieve less salient semantic knowledge was equivalent in the two groups.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's semantic assessments.

claim: The ability to retrieve less salient semantic knowledge was equivalent in young and older groups.
source: This manipulation had similar effects in young and older people, suggesting that the ability to retrieve less salient semantic knowledge was equivalent in the two groups.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the controlled retrieval findings.

claim: Older people showed a larger effect of the congruency manipulation in the semantic selection task.
source: Older people showed a larger effect of the congruency manipulation, performing more poorly in the incongruent condition.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's semantic assessments.

claim: Older people performed more poorly in the incongruent condition of the semantic selection task.
source: Older people showed a larger effect of the congruency manipulation, performing more poorly in the incongruent condition.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's semantic assessments.

claim: The older group had difficulty in selecting task-relevant semantic knowledge and inhibiting irrelevant associations.
source: This indicates that the older group had difficulty in selecting task-relevant semantic knowledge and inhibiting irrelevant associations.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the semantic selection task findings.

claim: Speech rate was influenced by age group, with older participants tending to speak more slowly.
source: Mixed effects modelling indicated that speech rate was influenced both by age group (B = −7.74, se = 3.81, p=0.046), with older participants tending to speak more slowly, and by task (B = −1.93, se = 0.79, p=0.016), with fewer words produced under dual-task conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's speech analysis with statistical support.

claim: Speech rate was influenced by task, with fewer words produced under dual-task conditions.
source: Mixed effects modelling indicated that speech rate was influenced both by age group (B = −7.74, se = 3.81, p=0.046), with older participants tending to speak more slowly, and by task (B = −1.93, se = 0.79, p=0.016), with fewer words produced under dual-task conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's speech analysis with statistical support.

claim: Cronbach's alpha was high for both global coherence (0.83) and local coherence (0.79) measures.
source: Cronbach's alpha was high for both measures (GC = 0.83; LC = 0.79), indicating that stable individual differences in coherence were present over the various topics about which participants were asked to speak.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's reliability analysis.

claim: Stable individual differences in coherence were present over the various topics about which participants were asked to speak.
source: Cronbach's alpha was high for both measures (GC = 0.83; LC = 0.79), indicating that stable individual differences in coherence were present over the various topics about which participants were asked to speak.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the reliability analysis.

claim: Global coherence and local coherence values were strongly correlated with one another (r = 0.79).
source: GC and LC values were also strongly correlated with one another (r = 0.79), suggesting that both are closely linked, as found in previous studies.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's correlation analysis.

claim: In the older group, age was negatively correlated with global coherence (r = −0.64).
source: In the older group, age was negatively correlated with GC (r = −0.64) and LC (r = −0.56).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's correlation analysis.

claim: In the older group, age was negatively correlated with local coherence (r = −0.56).
source: In the older group, age was negatively correlated with GC (r = −0.64) and LC (r = −0.56).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's correlation analysis.

claim: Older participants produced markedly less coherent speech than young people.
source: Age group was a strong predictor of GC: as predicted, older participants produced markedly less coherent speech than young people (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's mixed effects modeling and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The dual-task manipulation had no effect on global coherence.
source: As shown in Table 1, the dual-task manipulation had no effect on GC.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's mixed effects modeling and shown in Table 1.

claim: The interaction between age and task fell just short of statistical significance (p=0.052) for global coherence.
source: The interaction between age and task fell just short of statistical significance (p=0.052).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's mixed effects modeling.

claim: There may be a weak tendency for the effect of the task manipulation to be larger in older people.
source: This suggests that there may be a weak tendency for the effect of the task manipulation to be larger in older people.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the near-significant interaction.

claim: Speech rate was a negative predictor of global coherence.
source: Speech rate was a negative predictor of GC, indicating that participants who spoke more quickly showed a greater tendency to deviate from the topic being probed.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's mixed effects modeling.

claim: Participants who spoke more quickly showed a greater tendency to deviate from the topic being probed.
source: Speech rate was a negative predictor of GC, indicating that participants who spoke more quickly showed a greater tendency to deviate from the topic being probed.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the speech rate finding.

claim: Participants with a smaller ratio of Trails B to A had higher global coherence values.
source: As expected, participants with a smaller ratio of Trails B to A (indicating better executive ability) had higher GC values.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 2 of the mixed effects analysis.

claim: A significant difference in global coherence between the young and older groups remained after accounting for Trails ratio scores.
source: However, this was not sufficient to explain the lower GC values of older people: a significant difference between the young and older groups remained.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 2 of the mixed effects analysis.

claim: Participants with higher scores on the semantic selection test produced more coherent speech.
source: Participants with higher scores on the semantic selection test produced more coherent speech.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 3 of the mixed effects analysis.

claim: There was a tendency for individuals with higher semantic knowledge scores to produce less coherent speech.
source: there was also a tendency for individuals with higher semantic knowledge scores to produce less coherent speech.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 3 of the mixed effects analysis.

claim: Weak association task scores were not a significant predictor of global coherence.
source: Weak association task scores were not a significant predictor of GC.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 3 of the mixed effects analysis.

claim: There was no remaining effect of age group on global coherence after including semantic test scores in the model.
source: Importantly, there was no remaining effect of age group in this model (see Table 1), suggesting that lower levels of GC in older adults can be explained in terms of their lower semantic selection and higher semantic knowledge scores.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 3 of the mixed effects analysis and shown in Table 1.

claim: Lower levels of global coherence in older adults can be explained in terms of their lower semantic selection and higher semantic knowledge scores.
source: Importantly, there was no remaining effect of age group in this model (see Table 1), suggesting that lower levels of GC in older adults can be explained in terms of their lower semantic selection and higher semantic knowledge scores.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the finding that age effects disappeared after including semantic variables.

claim: Trails ratio was a significant predictor of local coherence.
source: In Model 2, Trails ratio was again a significant predictor of coherence, but a significant age effect remained.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 2 of the local coherence analysis.

claim: The age group effect on local coherence was not significant once semantic scores were included.
source: In contrast, the age group effect was not significant once semantic scores were included (Model 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 3 of the local coherence analysis.

claim: Scores on the semantic selection task were a significant predictor of local coherence.
source: Scores on the semantic selection task were a significant predictor of LC, with participants who performed poorly on this task tending to be less coherent (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 3 of the local coherence analysis and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Participants who performed poorly on the semantic selection task tended to be less coherent in local coherence.
source: Scores on the semantic selection task were a significant predictor of LC, with participants who performed poorly on this task tending to be less coherent (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Model 3 of the local coherence analysis and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Global coherence and local coherence loaded exclusively on Factor 2 in the principal components analysis.
source: GC and LC loaded exclusively on Factor 2, confirming that coherence emerged as a discrete characteristic of speech.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the principal components analysis.

claim: Coherence emerged as a discrete characteristic of speech.
source: GC and LC loaded exclusively on Factor 2, confirming that coherence emerged as a discrete characteristic of speech.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the principal components analysis.

claim: Factor 1 indexed the use of long, abstract, late-acquired words in speech.
source: Factor 1 indexed the use of long, abstract, late-acquired words in speech, so appeared to reflect access to complex vocabulary.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the principal components analysis results.

claim: Factor 1 appeared to reflect access to complex vocabulary.
source: Factor 1 indexed the use of long, abstract, late-acquired words in speech, so appeared to reflect access to complex vocabulary.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the principal components analysis results.

claim: High scores on Factor 3 were associated with use of low frequency, concrete nouns that were low in semantic diversity.
source: High scores on Factor 3 were associated with use of low frequency, concrete nouns that were low in semantic diversity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the principal components analysis results.

claim: Factor 3 may reflect the degree to which speech referenced highly specific concepts.
source: This factor may reflect the degree to which speech referenced highly specific concepts, so we labelled it semantic specificity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the principal components analysis results.

claim: High scores on Factor 4 were characterised by high type:token ratio and a low proportion of closed-class words.
source: Finally, high scores on Factor 4 were characterised by high type:token ratio and a low proportion of closed-class words, which are indicative of greater lexical diversity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the principal components analysis results.

claim: High type:token ratio and low proportion of closed-class words are indicative of greater lexical diversity.
source: Finally, high scores on Factor 4 were characterised by high type:token ratio and a low proportion of closed-class words, which are indicative of greater lexical diversity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about linguistic measures.

claim: Lower coherence was associated with poorer Trails performance.
source: The results for Factor 2 (coherence) were the same as previously observed for GC and LC separately: lower coherence was associated with poorer Trails and semantic selection performance but with better semantic knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the factor analysis.

claim: Lower coherence was associated with poorer semantic selection performance.
source: The results for Factor 2 (coherence) were the same as previously observed for GC and LC separately: lower coherence was associated with poorer Trails and semantic selection performance but with better semantic knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the factor analysis.

claim: Lower coherence was associated with better semantic knowledge.
source: The results for Factor 2 (coherence) were the same as previously observed for GC and LC separately: lower coherence was associated with poorer Trails and semantic selection performance but with better semantic knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the factor analysis.

claim: No other factor besides coherence showed the same pattern of associations with Trails, semantic selection, and semantic knowledge.
source: Importantly, no other factor showed the same pattern.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the factor analysis.

claim: Semantic knowledge was positively correlated with scores on Factor 1 (vocabulary).
source: The only other significant effects were that semantic knowledge was positively correlated with scores on factors 1 (vocabulary) and 4 (lexical diversity), indicating that participants with broader semantic knowledge used a broader and more complex range of vocabulary when speaking.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the factor analysis.

claim: Semantic knowledge was positively correlated with scores on Factor 4 (lexical diversity).
source: The only other significant effects were that semantic knowledge was positively correlated with scores on factors 1 (vocabulary) and 4 (lexical diversity), indicating that participants with broader semantic knowledge used a broader and more complex range of vocabulary when speaking.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the factor analysis.

claim: Participants with broader semantic knowledge used a broader and more complex range of vocabulary when speaking.
source: The only other significant effects were that semantic knowledge was positively correlated with scores on factors 1 (vocabulary) and 4 (lexical diversity), indicating that participants with broader semantic knowledge used a broader and more complex range of vocabulary when speaking.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the factor analysis findings.

claim: Participants' executive and semantic selection abilities had a specific effect on their coherence but not on other aspects of their speech production.
source: This analysis therefore confirms that the participants' executive and semantic selection abilities had a specific effect on their coherence but not on other aspects of their speech production.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the factor analysis.

claim: Older people had slower RTs on the secondary task than young people.
source: In brief, older people had slower RTs and both groups were slower when the task was combined with speaking.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the secondary task analysis.

claim: Both groups were slower on the secondary task when it was combined with speaking.
source: In brief, older people had slower RTs and both groups were slower when the task was combined with speaking.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the secondary task analysis.

claim: There was no interaction between age group and task condition for secondary task performance.
source: Importantly, however, there was no interaction between these factors, indicating that the requirement to perform two tasks affected both groups equally (see Appendix 5—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the secondary task analysis.

claim: The requirement to perform two tasks affected both groups equally.
source: Importantly, however, there was no interaction between these factors, indicating that the requirement to perform two tasks affected both groups equally (see Appendix 5—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the secondary task analysis.

claim: Participants' global and local coherence scores did not predict performance on the secondary task.
source: Participants' GC and LC scores did not predict performance on the secondary task, ruling out the possibility of a trade-off between secondary task performance and maintenance of coherence.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the secondary task analysis.

claim: There was no trade-off between secondary task performance and maintenance of coherence.
source: Participants' GC and LC scores did not predict performance on the secondary task, ruling out the possibility of a trade-off between secondary task performance and maintenance of coherence.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the secondary task analysis.

claim: The study replicated previous findings indicating that individuals with greater domain-general executive ability produce more coherent speech.
source: We replicated previous findings indicating that individuals with greater domain-general executive ability produce more coherent speech, but this effect did not fully account for age differences in coherence.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: Domain-general executive ability did not fully account for age differences in coherence.
source: We replicated previous findings indicating that individuals with greater domain-general executive ability produce more coherent speech, but this effect did not fully account for age differences in coherence.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: When semantic abilities were included as additional predictors of coherence, the age group difference was eliminated.
source: However, when we included semantic abilities as additional predictors of coherence, the age group difference was eliminated.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: Semantic selection ability emerged as a positive predictor of coherence.
source: Semantic selection ability emerged as a positive predictor of coherence while breadth of semantic knowledge was a negative predictor.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: Breadth of semantic knowledge was a negative predictor of coherence.
source: Semantic selection ability emerged as a positive predictor of coherence while breadth of semantic knowledge was a negative predictor.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: The effects of semantic abilities on coherence were specific to coherence and not to other characteristics of speech.
source: These effects were specific to coherence and not to other characteristics of speech, and were not attributable to differences in speech rate.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: The effects of semantic abilities on coherence were not attributable to differences in speech rate.
source: These effects were specific to coherence and not to other characteristics of speech, and were not attributable to differences in speech rate.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: Older people produce less coherent speech because they are less skilled at selecting the most relevant aspects of semantic knowledge to include in their speech.
source: Our results indicate that older people produce less coherent speech (a) because they are less skilled at selecting the most relevant aspects of semantic knowledge to include in their speech and (b) because they have a larger set of semantic knowledge to select from.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: Older people produce less coherent speech because they have a larger set of semantic knowledge to select from.
source: Our results indicate that older people produce less coherent speech (a) because they are less skilled at selecting the most relevant aspects of semantic knowledge to include in their speech and (b) because they have a larger set of semantic knowledge to select from.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: The monitoring and control of discourse is influenced by the function of the semantic system, in addition to domain-general executive resources.
source: First and foremost, our results establish that the monitoring and control of discourse is influenced by the function of the semantic system, in addition to domain-general executive resources.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings in the Discussion.

claim: Coherent communication requires the speaker to select the subset of information which is directly relevant at the current time, while suppressing aspects of knowledge that are activated but less pertinent.
source: Coherent communication requires the speaker to select the subset of that information which is directly relevant at the current time, while suppressing aspects of knowledge that are activated but less pertinent.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: Selection demands grow as the narrative develops and new associations are activated.
source: These demands grow as the narrative develops and new associations are activated.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: Episodic and semantic memories are mutually interdependent.
source: The prompts used in the present study were designed to elicit general knowledge rather than specific personal experiences. However, episodic and semantic memories are mutually interdependent (Binder et al., 2009), and it was clear that participants drew on both in generating their responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: It was clear that participants drew on both episodic and semantic memories in generating their responses.
source: The prompts used in the present study were designed to elicit general knowledge rather than specific personal experiences. However, episodic and semantic memories are mutually interdependent (Binder et al., 2009), and it was clear that participants drew on both in generating their responses.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Selection mechanisms for episodic and semantic memories are likely shared to some degree.
source: It is likely that selection mechanisms for these distinct types of memory are shared to some degree.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical speculation.

claim: The left mid ventrolateral prefrontal cortex responds to selection demands in semantic, episodic, and working memory domains.
source: Indeed, the left mid ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC), the brain region most closely associated with semantic selection, responds to selection demands in all three domains (Badre and Wagner, 2007; Dobbins and Wagner, 2005; King et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The requirement to selectively recall particular details of an event drives greater activation in left mid VLPFC.
source: The requirement to selectively recall particular details of an event drives greater activation in left mid VLPFC, suggesting that this area also mediates selection from episodic memory (Badre and Wagner, 2007; Dobbins and Wagner, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The monitoring and selection of retrieved episodic memories is associated with activation of dorsolateral prefrontal regions that are not implicated in selection from semantic knowledge.
source: However, the monitoring and selection of retrieved episodic memories is also associated with activation of dorsolateral prefrontal regions that are not implicated in selection from semantic knowledge (Fletcher et al., 1998; Rugg et al., 2003), which may indicate a degree of independence between semantic and episodic selection at the neural level.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: There may be a degree of independence between semantic and episodic selection at the neural level.
source: However, the monitoring and selection of retrieved episodic memories is also associated with activation of dorsolateral prefrontal regions that are not implicated in selection from semantic knowledge (Fletcher et al., 1998; Rugg et al., 2003), which may indicate a degree of independence between semantic and episodic selection at the neural level.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on neuroimaging findings.

claim: Patients with deficits in semantic selection also find it hard to resolve interference in episodic memory tasks.
source: At a behavioural level, recent work indicates that patients with deficits in semantic selection also find it hard to resolve interference in episodic memory tasks (Stampacchia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Healthy older people often show increased interference from irrelevant events when retrieving episodic memories.
source: In addition, healthy older people often show increased interference from irrelevant events when retrieving episodic memories (Campbell et al., 2010; Ikier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: These findings point to a more general old-age deficit in selecting the most task-relevant aspects of retrieved semantic and episodic knowledge.
source: Combined with our previous study (Hoffman, 2018), these findings point to a more general old-age deficit in selecting the most task-relevant aspects of retrieved semantic and episodic knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The selection deficit contributes to the loss of coherence in later life.
source: We have demonstrated here that this selection deficit contributes to the loss of coherence in later life.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Lateral prefrontal cortex exhibits the greatest reductions in cortical volume as a function of age.
source: Lateral prefrontal cortex exhibits the greatest reductions in cortical volume as a function of age (Fjell et al., 2009; Raz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Older adults activated the left VLPFC region less strongly than young people during semantic processing.
source: In addition, a recent meta-analysis of 47 functional neuroimaging studies found that older adults activated this region less strongly than young people during semantic processing (Hoffman and Morcom, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The measure of executive ability derived from the Trails test was not correlated with performance on the semantic selection task.
source: The measure of executive ability derived from this test was not correlated with performance on the semantic selection task (young group: r = 0.08; older group: r = 0.02)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's correlation analysis.

claim: Trails performance was a strong predictor of coherence.
source: and, although Trails performance was a strong predictor of coherence, we found that semantic selection had an additional, independent effect.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's mixed effects modeling.

claim: Semantic selection had an additional, independent effect on coherence beyond Trails performance.
source: and, although Trails performance was a strong predictor of coherence, we found that semantic selection had an additional, independent effect.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's mixed effects modeling.

claim: The relationship between coherence and semantic selection cannot simply be attributed to poorer general executive ability.
source: This suggests that the relationship between coherence and semantic selection cannot simply be attributed to poorer general executive ability.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the independence of semantic selection and Trails effects.

claim: The Trails test primarily taps shifting (or task-switching) ability.
source: The Trails test primarily taps shifting (or task-switching) ability (Arbuthnott and Frank, 2000; Hedden and Yoon, 2006; Sánchez-Cubillo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Semantic selection deficits in later life may be related to more general declines in inhibitory function.
source: This is an important issue to resolve if we are to understand how semantic selection processes relate to domain-general executive function, particularly as semantic selection deficits in later life may be related to more general declines in inhibitory function, which have been reported across a range of tasks (Borella et al., 2008; Hasher and Zacks, 1988; Hoffman, 2018; Salthouse and Meinz, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with supporting citations.

claim: More general declines in inhibitory function have been reported across a range of tasks in older adults.
source: This is an important issue to resolve if we are to understand how semantic selection processes relate to domain-general executive function, particularly as semantic selection deficits in later life may be related to more general declines in inhibitory function, which have been reported across a range of tasks (Borella et al., 2008; Hasher and Zacks, 1988; Hoffman, 2018; Salthouse and Meinz, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Individuals with a wider range of lexical-semantic knowledge tended to be less coherent.
source: We also found that the breadth of participants' semantic knowledge influenced their coherence. Individuals with a wider range of lexical-semantic knowledge tended to be less coherent.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Selecting appropriately from activated knowledge is critical to maintaining coherence.
source: This effect is consistent with the notion that selecting appropriately from activated knowledge is critical to maintaining coherence.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: The challenge of selecting appropriately from activated knowledge becomes greater the more information one has in one's semantic store.
source: This challenge becomes greater the more information one has in one's semantic store, simply because more concepts are likely to be activated in response to any given cue.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: Being more knowledgeable in itself brings greater challenges in identifying the most relevant aspects of knowledge to use in speech.
source: Thus, our data indicate that being more knowledgeable in itself brings greater challenges in identifying the most relevant aspects of knowledge to use in speech.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Older people have greater semantic and general world knowledge.
source: It is very well-established that older people have greater semantic and general world knowledge, as was the case in our study (Rönnlund et al., 2005; Salthouse, 2004; Verhaeghen, 2003)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations and confirmed by the study's data.

claim: Greater semantic knowledge may have contributed to age-related coherence declines.
source: so this factor may also have contributed to age-related coherence declines.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the findings.

claim: Breadth of semantic knowledge predicted the use of more sophisticated vocabulary.
source: It is also worth noting that breadth of semantic knowledge also predicted the use of more sophisticated vocabulary (i.e., more late-acquired, abstract nouns) and greater lexical diversity (for a similar result, see Kemper and Sumner, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study with a supporting citation.

claim: Breadth of semantic knowledge predicted greater lexical diversity.
source: It is also worth noting that breadth of semantic knowledge also predicted the use of more sophisticated vocabulary (i.e., more late-acquired, abstract nouns) and greater lexical diversity (for a similar result, see Kemper and Sumner, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study with a supporting citation.

claim: Quantity of semantic knowledge has more global effects on the characteristics of speech, unlike semantic selection, which impacts specifically on coherence.
source: Therefore, it appears that quantity of semantic knowledge has more global effects on the characteristics of speech, unlike semantic selection, which impacts specifically on coherence.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Conditions of divided attention had no overall effect on the coherence of speech.
source: We found that conditions of divided attention had no overall effect on the coherence of speech, in contrast to the findings of Kemper et al., 2010.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: The secondary task in this study appeared less demanding than that used by Kemper and colleagues.
source: However, we note that our secondary task appeared less demanding that that used by Kemper and colleagues.
evidence: This is stated as an observation comparing the study's methods to previous research.

claim: The secondary task produced a reduction in speech rate of around 5 WPM in this study.
source: Our secondary task produced a reduction in speech rate of around 5 WPM, compared with 20–40 WPM in Kemper et al.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: The secondary task in Kemper et al. produced a reduction in speech rate of 20-40 WPM.
source: Our secondary task produced a reduction in speech rate of around 5 WPM, compared with 20–40 WPM in Kemper et al.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous research.

claim: There was a non-significant trend (p=0.056) towards an interaction of dual-task demands with age for global coherence.
source: Despite this, we did find a non-significant trend (p=0.056) towards an interaction of dual-task demands with age (for the GC measure).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: There was a suggestion that the secondary task may have had a small effect on the coherence of older people, while young people appeared unaffected.
source: There was a suggestion that the secondary task may have had a small effect on the coherence of older people, while young people appeared unaffected (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There remains a possibility that divided attention has a particular detrimental effect on coherence in older adults.
source: There remains a possibility therefore that divided attention has a particular detrimental effect on coherence in older adults.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the near-significant trend.

claim: Previous studies have found varying effects of age on coherence, depending on the speech elicitation task used.
source: Previous studies have found varying effects of age on coherence, depending on the speech elicitation task used.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous research.

claim: Narratives elicited from verbal prompts reveal the greatest decrements in coherence.
source: Typically, narratives elicited from verbal prompts, as in the present study, reveal the greatest decrements in coherence while tasks that elicit speech using visual stimuli, such as picture descriptions or story-telling from comic strips, produce smaller effects (James et al., 1998; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous research with supporting citations.

claim: Tasks that elicit speech using visual stimuli produce smaller effects on coherence than verbal prompts.
source: Typically, narratives elicited from verbal prompts, as in the present study, reveal the greatest decrements in coherence while tasks that elicit speech using visual stimuli, such as picture descriptions or story-telling from comic strips, produce smaller effects (James et al., 1998; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous research with supporting citations.

claim: When a pictured stimulus is used to cue speech, it acts as a source of constraint over semantic activation.
source: When a pictured stimulus is used to cue speech, it acts as a source of constraint over semantic activation.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical explanation for task differences.

claim: Constructing a response to a brief verbal prompt is a trickier proposition than responding to a pictured stimulus, since a wide range of potentially relevant information may be activated and no external cues are available to guide selection.
source: In contrast, constructing a response to a brief verbal prompt is a trickier proposition, since a wide range of potentially relevant information may be activated and no external cues are available to guide selection.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical explanation for task differences.

claim: The monologues elicited in the present study are a rather extreme example of the phenomenon of unconstrained semantic activation.
source: Of course, the monologues elicited in the present study are a rather extreme example of this phenomenon.
evidence: This is stated as a reflection on the study's methods.

claim: In everyday conversational speech, environmental cues are often available to guide the selection of speech content.
source: In everyday conversational speech, environmental cues are often available to guide the selection of speech content.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about conversation.

claim: Speakers with poor coherence are less skilled at interpreting social cues.
source: Such cues can only be effective if speakers are sensitive to them, however, and evidence suggests that speakers with poor coherence are also less skilled at interpreting social cues (Pushkar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Greater coherence is not always a desirable characteristic for speech.
source: Finally, it is important to consider an underlying assumption often made in the literature on coherence: that greater coherence is always a desirable characteristic for speech.
evidence: This is stated as a critical reflection on assumptions in the literature.

claim: Individuals who are less coherent in conversation perform poorly at communicating task-related information to a partner in an experimental setting.
source: For example, there is evidence that individuals who are less coherent in conversation perform poorly at communicating task-related information to a partner in an experimental setting (Arbuckle et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: When the goal of a conversation is to entertain, a less focused approach to speech may have its advantages.
source: In other situations, however, a less focused approach to speech may have its advantages. When the goal of a conversation is to entertain, rather than to convey specific information, the ability to shift focus away from the original topic may be beneficial.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about the benefits of lower coherence in certain contexts.

claim: Older people are generally considered to produce more enjoyable stories than young people.
source: Indeed, older people are generally considered to produce more enjoyable stories than young people (Ryan et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Older people produced more off-topic speech than young people in a study by James et al. (1998).
source: One notable study collected responses of young and older people to questions about life events and asked judges to rate them on various dimensions (James et al., 1998). Older people produced more off-topic speech than young people and their narratives were rated as less focused.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Older people's narratives were rated as less focused than young people's in a study by James et al. (1998).
source: One notable study collected responses of young and older people to questions about life events and asked judges to rate them on various dimensions (James et al., 1998). Older people produced more off-topic speech than young people and their narratives were rated as less focused.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Less coherent speakers were rated as less clear and focused in a study by James et al. (1998).
source: However, while less coherent speakers were rated as less clear and focused, they were also considered to be more interesting and to have produced better stories.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Less coherent speakers were considered to be more interesting and to have produced better stories in a study by James et al. (1998).
source: However, while less coherent speakers were rated as less clear and focused, they were also considered to be more interesting and to have produced better stories.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: The ability to communicate coherently is critical in many but not all everyday conversations.
source: In summary, the ability to communicate coherently is critical in many but not all everyday conversations.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the discussion of context-dependent coherence.

claim: The most effective communicators may be those who can tailor their selection of content to the current situational demands.
source: It is possible that the most effective communicators are those who can tailor their selection of content to the current situational demands, focusing tightly on the subject at hand when required to but broadening their focus at other times.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about effective communication.

claim: Little is known at present about how coherence interacts with situational demands.
source: Little is known at present about how coherence interacts with these situational demands and this is one area where more research is needed.
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Thirty young adults, aged between 18 and 30 (mean = 19.3), were recruited from the undergraduate Psychology course at the University of Edinburgh.
source: Thirty young adults, aged between 18 and 30 (mean = 19.3), were recruited from the undergraduate Psychology course at the University of Edinburgh and participated in the study in exchange for course credit.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's participants.

claim: Thirty older adults, aged between 61 and 91 (mean = 76.0), were recruited from the Psychology department's volunteer panel.
source: Thirty older adults, aged between 61 and 91 (mean = 76.0), were recruited from the Psychology department's volunteer panel.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's participants.

claim: All participants reported to be in good health with no history of neurological or psychiatric illness.
source: All participants reported to be in good health with no history of neurological or psychiatric illness.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's participants.

claim: Young and older adults did not differ significantly in years of education completed.
source: Young and older adults did not differ significantly in years of education completed (t(58) = 0.93, p=0.36).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study's demographic analysis.

claim: The study was approved by the University of Edinburgh Psychology Research Ethics Committee (120-1415/3).
source: All participants provided informed consent and the study was approved by the University of Edinburgh Psychology Research Ethics Committee (120-1415/3).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's ethical approval.

claim: A ratio rather than a difference score was used for Trails performance as this measure minimises the influence of differences in general processing speed.
source: A ratio rather than a difference score was used as this measure minimises the influence of differences in general processing speed (Arbuthnott and Frank, 2000; Salthouse, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological decision with supporting citations.

claim: Scores on the lexical decision and synonym matching tasks were strongly correlated.
source: As scores on these tasks were strongly correlated, they were averaged to give a single measure of breadth of semantic knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as a finding that justified combining the measures.

claim: The Weak Association condition was assumed to place greater demands on controlled retrieval of semantic information.
source: The Weak Association condition was assumed to place greater demands on controlled retrieval of semantic information, because automatic spreading of activation in the semantic network would not be sufficient to identify the correct response (Badre and Wagner, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical assumption about the task with a supporting citation.

claim: Incongruent trials placed high demands on semantic selection processes because there was no pre-existing semantic relationship between probe and target to boost activation of the target.
source: Incongruent trials placed high demands on semantic selection processes for two reasons: first, because there was no pre-existing semantic relationship between probe and target to boost activation of the target and second, because the strong but irrelevant relationship between the probe and foil had to be ignored.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical explanation of the task design.

claim: Incongruent trials placed high demands on semantic selection processes because the strong but irrelevant relationship between the probe and foil had to be ignored.
source: Incongruent trials placed high demands on semantic selection processes for two reasons: first, because there was no pre-existing semantic relationship between probe and target to boost activation of the target and second, because the strong but irrelevant relationship between the probe and foil had to be ignored.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical explanation of the task design.

claim: Participants were asked to speak for 60 s at a time in response to a written prompt.
source: On speech-only trials, participants were asked to speak for 60 s at a time in response to a written prompt (for full list of prompts, see Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's methods.

claim: Prompts were designed to probe particular areas of semantic knowledge.
source: Prompts were designed to probe particular areas of semantic knowledge (e.g., What sort of things do you have to do to look after a dog?).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's methods.

claim: On dual-task trials, participants were asked to complete an attention-demanding secondary task while speaking.
source: On dual-task trials, participants were asked to complete an attention-demanding secondary task while speaking (Craik et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's methods with a supporting citation.

claim: Seven speech samples were obtained in the speech-only condition and seven in the dual-task condition.
source: Seven speech samples were obtained in the speech-only condition and seven in the dual-task condition.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's methods.

claim: The study used latent semantic analysis (LSA) to generate measures of local and global coherence.
source: Measures of local and global coherence were generated using an automated computational linguistic approach. Analyses were implemented in R; the code is publicly available and can easily be applied to new samples (https://osf.io/8atfn/). Our approach used latent semantic analysis (LSA) (Landauer and Dumais, 1997)
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's methods with a supporting citation.

claim: LSA is a computational technique in which patterns of word co-occurrence are used to construct a high-dimensional semantic space.
source: Our approach used latent semantic analysis (LSA) (Landauer and Dumais, 1997), one of a number of computational techniques in which patterns of word co-occurrence are used to construct a high-dimensional semantic space.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the LSA method with a supporting citation.

claim: Words that are used in similar contexts are assigned similar vectors in LSA.
source: Data reduction techniques are then applied to this matrix, with the result that each word is represented as a high-dimensional vector. Words that are used in similar contexts (and are thus assumed to have related meanings) are assigned similar vectors.
evidence: This is stated as a description of how LSA works.

claim: Word similarities derived from LSA are strong predictors of human judgements of semantic relatedness.
source: Word similarities derived in this way are strong predictors of human judgements of semantic relatedness and human performance on a range of tasks (Bullinaria and Levy, 2007; Recchia and Jones, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Vectors for individual words can be combined linearly to represent the meanings of whole sentences and passages of speech/text.
source: Importantly, vectors for individual words can be combined linearly to represent the meanings of whole sentences and passages of speech/text (Foltz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Researchers have used LSA to generate estimates of coherence for texts or spoken samples.
source: A number of researchers have used this property to generate estimates of coherence for texts or spoken samples based on LSA similarity measures (Elvevåg et al., 2007; Foltz, 2007; Foltz et al., 1998; Graesser et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Each speech sample was divided into smaller windows of 20 words each.
source: The overall strategy we took was to divide each speech sample into smaller windows (of 20 words each) and to use LSA to generate vector representations of the semantic content of each window.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's methods.

claim: Local coherence was defined as the cosine similarity of the semantic vector for the current window with that of the previous window.
source: Local coherence was defined as the cosine similarity of the semantic vector for the current window with that of the previous window.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's methods.

claim: Global coherence was defined as similarity of the vector for each window with the composite vector derived from the other participants' responses.
source: Global coherence was defined as similarity of the vector for each window with the composite vector derived from the other participants' responses.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the study's methods.

claim: There was a strong correlation between rated global coherence and LSA-based global coherence (r = 0.68).
source: The LSA-based coherence measures were validated by comparing them with judgements of coherence provided by human raters for a subset of speech samples (see Appendix 4 for details). There was a strong correlation between rated GC and LSA-based GC (r = 0.68) and a somewhat weaker relationship between LSA-based LC and LC ratings (r = 0.37).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the validation analysis.

claim: There was a somewhat weaker relationship between LSA-based local coherence and local coherence ratings (r = 0.37).
source: The LSA-based coherence measures were validated by comparing them with judgements of coherence provided by human raters for a subset of speech samples (see Appendix 4 for details). There was a strong correlation between rated GC and LSA-based GC (r = 0.68) and a somewhat weaker relationship between LSA-based LC and LC ratings (r = 0.37).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the validation analysis.

claim: Test-retest reliability of the coherence measures was high.
source: Test-retest reliability was high (see Appendix 4).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the reliability analysis.
